newsitem.title: USA: Lawsuit says America Online spreads child porn.
newsitem.headline: Lawsuit says America Online spreads child porn.

text.p: A Florida woman is suing America Online, saying the Internet service allowed a subscriber to market pornographic pictures of her 11-year-old son and two other boys to pedophiles, her lawyer said on Friday.

AOL had created "a home shopping network for pedophiles and child pornographers," alleged the lawsuit filed on Thursday at a West Palm Beach circuit court. It said AOL was responsible for the content of the material available on its services but had failed to enforce its rules and monitor its subscribers.

One subscriber, former Palm Beach schoolteacher Ron Russell, who is named in the suit, was convicted of an array of sexual charges. "He says he used public channels to exchange phone numbers, tapes and photographs and to distribute them who knows where," said Brian Smith, attorney for the woman plaintiff, identified only as Jane Doe.
"Our claim is that America Online created a marketplace for pedophiles and child pornographers," he told Reuters.

Russell allegedly used the service to sell images of sexual acts involving himself, the woman's 11-year-old son and two other boys he had befriended in 1994. Material was advertised on AOL's electronic chat rooms with titles such as "Trading Teen Pics" and "Young Boys for You."

The suit claims $8 million -- a sum Smith said was chosen because AOL, the world's largest online service, said it had 8 million subscribers. "How can you put a figure on the humiliation and mental anguish suffered?" he asked.

The suit said AOL prohibited its members from transmitting objectional, obscene or illegal material but had failed to police them adequately. "AOL service became known to the pedophile community as a place for open discussion, trading and marketing of child pornography ... in essence AOL Inc. has created a home shopping network for pedophiles and child pornographers," it said.
It added that AOL had ignored complaints concerning Russell and its chat rooms carried exchanges of addresses and telephone numbers for the sale of pornograhic material.

Russell was arrested in February 1995 after a federal investigation into a ring of men, several of them teachers, who swapped child pornography by computer. He is now serving a 22-year sentence for attempted sexual battery and a 14-year sentence on child pornography charges.
An AOL spokesman said the company made every effort to keep pornography and objectionable material off the service.
"I can't comment directly on the case but the bottom line is America Online has no tolerance for this kind of activity," Andrew Graziani said from the company's headquarters in Virginia.
"The idea that America Online is a safe haven for illegal acts is simply not true. Unfortunately there are some people who will break the law. Illegal acts of this kind are beyond the pale," he said.
He said AOL terminated accounts of people who broke its rules and worked closely with law enforcement. It was studying the lawsuit to prepare a response.
